item.content:encoded:
I very much enjoyed this one. It is a good idea with good content, but there are a number of missing commas that thoroughly confused me. I had to reread several sentences before I realized what was going on in them.

I also think that the way the article went from the UIU file to the addendum was confusing. I think either the order of them need to be switched (which would likely cause some narrative issues), or there should be some greater indication between the two. As is, the UIU file has plenty of bolding in it itself, so when the interview came I thought it was still a part of the file.

My last complaint is that the containment procedures say to keep the SCPs knowledge to the 70's, but if it has gotten into the foundations databases before, it certainly has advanced information. We even see its knowledge of the modern world during the interview when it mentions the man in the stall masturbating by pointing out the fact that he's on a phone. If it was really stuck in the 70's, it probably wouldn't know what that rectangle of light was.

But my complaints aside, I did enjoy the SCP. It's a good concept with good content to back it up.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Okay, I sat on it for a few days, but here's a blow-by-blow as I read back through the article, trying to type out my thoughts as I had them.

+ It's really long
- I warned you

As the original usable software library of the machines have been completely used

'has'

researchers are to enter the SCP-633 containment area to drain them of fluids

I'm not sure what 'them' refers to in this sentence. 633 itself is a phenomenon, not any number of physical objects; it's not clear what's meant to be happening here.

An understanding of late 1970’s technology and cultural references is necessary to prevent accidental introduction of banned ideas to SCP-633.

So this is the actual hook. We get a bit of this idea in the first paragraph of containment, but whatever this is, we now know the Foundation is trying to keep it stuck in the 70's.

all computational devices post-1979

This would read just a tad better with 'created' in there.

Okay, so 633 is now a phenomenon (I still don't think you need 'supernatural', it sounds unprofessional somehow, and we already know it's gonna be supernatural or else the Foundation wouldn't care) that resembles a computer virus, that's an interesting change.

By "near-contact", I assume this means that you can't use an infected computer while wearing gloves? Would this mean the biohazard suits really don't do anything?

it is unknown what information was input

I think you should specify the extent of information. We know there was information input into it, that's the sum total of its "imited information about the outside world". There's just no way to know precisely how limited that limit is.

So now I see that "Ghost" is essentially an AI, some kind of consciousness that inhabits computers. Okay.

I absolutely detest seeing words like "ectoplasmic" in SCPs, but that might just be me. Like, seriously, who they gonna call?

Okay, so the 5m infection perimeter off the fluids is what qualifies as "near-contact", right? This might be worth specifying when it's first mentioned, and then here, you say, oh yeah, the fluids are a contaminant vector as well as the machinery. And I still have to wonder if the biohazard suits are enough… but I'd imagine they are, or else they wouldn't be included in the containment procedures. Okay.

Production of fluids (why aren't these designated SCP-633-1? That would simplify things a lot…) has increased since containment? Interesting…

biological tissue and cloth

I suggest switching these, unless you're talking about biological cloth. :B

So infected humans can be decontaminated? I guess there's still a risk of 633 getting out of its containment area, so risking it isn't worth it. I'm now wondering what an effected human looks like…

I love "will frequently attempt to impress the user". I mean, what's essentially a sentient computer program having a modus operandi of going, "Look what I can do! :D" is adorable. Also, trying to avoid anxiety with broad praise, nice touch.

Had to look up polymorphic code to see if that was a thing. <.< It is.

Oh boy, a crosslink. And it's to an article that's kind of exactly the same thing. :/ (Though at least without interactions with two of the highest-rated articles in the wiki's history…)

Okay, so this screw. The AI isn't just an AI, because its consciousness can spread via a single nonmechanical object. Is that what infection is like? It's not "Here I am in this screw now! Gosh, this is different!" It's that a screw, or a human, or another computer, can pick up the 633 infection and spread it to other things, with the end result, if you will, being getting to another computer, where it can then communicate with people as a software program.

But even the fact that it can stay in recycled metal is crazy. I guess the IT department shouldn't feel too bad. I mean, I'd think that destroying an infected component would destroy the infection. So that's another detail that makes this interesting, and dangerous.

I still find it hard to believe that any federal information act would also include stuff from the UIU. Or maybe they just don't have as hard a duty to normalcy as the Foundation? I like that they're included, regardless.

I love that they fucking made a "][" with the brackets, like goddammit, the UIU is full of nerds.

Eyes> Green(?)

Oh my god what.

Okay, they address that incineration is not enough to prevent infection.

as such a chemical solution is to be employed which can be obtained from Professor Tamlin.

This one took me a minute. The comma before this sentence needs to be a semicolon; then you need a comma after 'such', and a comma after 'employed'. Unless you're trying to make it look like the UIU can't pay a proofreader, in which case, you need a few more errors in the file. :V

So the UIU considers it malevolent? Interesting. Makes me wonder what changed to make it more childlike, or if it's just biding its time in Foundation custody. Also interesting in that its power is considerably more dangerous 40 years on.

Hey, yoric's sloppy expunger has been here! :V Are the bits of that name meant to evoke anything?

Damn, Rosen, learn to use question marks. >:V

The Ghost is ready.

I like this a lot more than its usual opening line.

Please do not answer QUESTION with QUESTION.

This is neat, too.

Okay, I think everyone was confused by the 'yoruself' line because they didn't realize it was being typed. With that detail firmly in mind, it says volumes.

So the little bugger has interfaced with every computer in the site, despite all attempts to keep it from doing so. Furthermore, it doesn't realize that this interface would allow it to essentially control everything; it's just peeking in on people. Again, dangerous, and something we are just barely able to keep under control.

This anomaly has repeatedly run circles around our IT department and really, I'm very disappointed in their performance.

The whole final note leaves a bad taste in my mouth, and this line especially. Like, what the hell does she expect them to do? They fucked up with the screw, sure, but this is less an infotech problem than a physical contaminants problems. Is it just me? I feel like this department is being unfairly blamed.

Anyway, at this point, I'm up to "downvote rescinded". The danger quotient ramps up nice and steady, but overall, I just don't find it that interesting. It's better than 079, to be sure, but we've already got 079. I stand by my claim that we need more of its personality or something to make it more interesting. Otherwise, it's just your average super-powerful computer virus that the Foundation is powerless to stand in the way of.

I was unsure whether the spag errors in the interview and UIU report were intentional and indicative that 633 was still affecting the system from within or if they're just oversights until the comments section, so - that's a thing. Perhaps that aspect of the piece was too subtle for me to grasp.

Other than that, it's pretty well constructed, as previously indicated - the graphic's high quality, the FBI's perspective feels appropriately 'X-Filey' in that this definitely qualifies as one of those unassuming-but-deadly skips that could easily fit into the sweet spot where they come in, and it leaves off on a nice bit of fridge logic. I don't really have strong thoughts on it one way or another; it was an enjoyable article with not too much chaff.

item.content:encoded:
The highly contagious weird property with the ectoplasm felt like misdirection that made the computer's disarming personality a more effective twist. I liked the interview log, where the little guy just wants to impress his friend and doesn't know he's doing anything wrong.

The UIU file was cool, I always like to see how different GOIs react to objects. I think it would help the readability of the article if this and the interview were behind labeled blocks — I'm not sure if that's possible with all the formatting on the UIU report, and it's a minor thing anyway, but seeing the addenda laid out up front would have helped it all come across more immediately for me.

All in all I love it though. It would be fun to do a tale where things go terribly wrong with their network and they have to ask The Ghost for help getting it under control (or a simulation where they make it think that's happening) — I bet it would just love to help out its buddies however it could, and try really hard to stay focused and not mess with any of the shiny, fun-looking things it saw along the way…

item.content:encoded:
I'm not really sure about this one. It has all the qualities of a successful article- good use of images, consistent clinical tone, solid pacing, a very ominous undertone- but somewhere in the middle it starts to feel disconnected, and by the end I felt slightly empty. As if there's not really a whole lot going on.

Perhaps I'm just being dense, but whatever narrative is being formed here doesn't feel as though it's been presented with much clarity. There's this overwhelming feeling of 'we should be scared of this thing' riddled throughout the article, yet even upon re-reading I couldn't really figure out why. Maybe my lack of knowledge regarding all of the terminology has killed my understanding of how this SCP works, or maybe you just haven't delivered on the hype (for lack of a better term) being built up through the documents successfully.

In short, I can't really put into words what I dislike about this article. For that reason, I'm going to have to settle on a no vote for now.
